blocks.text: Farmed salmon may be delivering fewer omega-3 fatty acids than older dietary guidance assumes
A small USDA-led study links the decline to a shift from fish-based feed toward crops and oils. The researchers say broader sampling is needed before dietary advice changes.

blocks.caption: Of salmon eaten worldwide is farmed
blocks.text: Nearly 70%

items: THE IDEA — New research suggests omega-3 levels in farmed salmon have fallen considerably, potentially weakening the nutritional basis for some advice to eat it.
WHY NOW — Farmed salmon production tripled between 2000 and 2020 as demand for seafood marketed as healthy increased.
WHAT CHANGES — Feed has shifted from smaller fish toward soy, canola and other land-grown ingredients as marine resources became more depleted.
THE CATCH — The study was not large enough to justify changing government guidance, and crop-based feed brings its own land-use and emissions costs.

blocks.text: The nutritional trade-off reflects a broader production shift: replacing pressure on small fish and marine ecosystems with greater reliance on cropland, including soy linked to deforestation concerns. In Europe and the UK, other research found that this change doubled farmed fish’s emissions per kilogram from 2000 to 2020.

The result is not that farmed salmon has become nutritionally worthless. It is that older figures may no longer describe the product consistently—and that expanding supply can move environmental pressures rather than remove them.

blocks.text: Farmed salmon may be losing some of the nutritional advantage that made it popular, new research suggests

A USDA-led study found that omega-3 levels in farmed salmon have fallen as producers replace small fish in feed with crops and oils. The sample was limited, so the researchers say broader evidence is needed before dietary advice changes.

blocks.caption: Of salmon eaten is farmed
blocks.text: Nearly 70%

items: THE IDEA — Farmed salmon supplies most of the salmon people eat, and production tripled between 2000 and 2020.
WHY NOW — New research suggests its omega-3 content has declined enough to make older nutrition figures less reliable.
WHAT CHANGES — Feed has shifted from smaller marine fish toward soy, canola and other land-based ingredients as oceans lose small fish.
THE CATCH — Crop-based feed reduces pressure on forage fish but brings other costs, including deforestation and higher emissions.

blocks.text: The mechanism is straightforward: salmon naturally eat other fish, but using those fish as feed became harder to sustain. Producers responded by using more crops and oils, which contain less of the omega-3 fatty acids associated with salmon’s health benefits. A 2016 study reported a similar trend.

The result is a trade-off rather than a simple improvement. Marine feed pressures smaller fish populations, while crop-based feed can shift environmental impacts onto land. In Norway, marine ingredients made up about 90 percent of feed ingredients in 1990, compared with about 23 percent in 2020.

The study is not large enough to justify changing government guidance, which recommends at least 8 ounces of fish a week and encourages salmon as an omega-3-rich choice. The researchers call for a broader, more representative study.

blocks.text: After 8 years, Europe's BepiColombo mission is on final approach to Mercury
The spacecraft has used plasma propulsion and repeated planetary flybys to prepare for a difficult orbital arrival later this year.

blocks.caption: Time since launch in 2018
blocks.text: 8 years

items: THE IDEA — BepiColombo is entering the final stretch of its journey to Mercury, the Solar System's innermost planet.
WHY NOW — A major milestone this week puts the mission on course for its final encounter later this year.
WHAT CHANGES — The spacecraft must arrive at just the right speed for Mercury's gravity to capture it into orbit.
THE CATCH — Reaching Mercury and slowing into orbit requires more energy than sending a probe on a flyby to distant Pluto.

blocks.text: Led by the European Space Agency, with contributions from Japan and the United States, the nearly $2 billion mission launched in 2018. It has spiraled inward using plasma propulsion and flybys of Earth, Venus, and Mercury, each maneuver changing its velocity and trajectory.
Mercury is close to the Sun, but getting there—and matching its speed—is the hard part.

Interplanetary missions often demand patience: NASA's New Horizons took nearly 10 years to reach Pluto. BepiColombo's route shows why a nearer destination can still require more energy when the goal is not merely to pass by, but to enter orbit.
The mission's next Mercury encounter will test whether eight years of carefully managed propulsion and flybys have delivered the spacecraft to the narrow speed range needed for capture.

blocks.text: After 8 years, Europe's BepiColombo mission is on final approach to Mercury
The spacecraft has used electric propulsion and planetary flybys to shed and redirect enough velocity for Mercury to capture it into orbit later this year.

blocks.caption: Its interplanetary journey since launch
blocks.text: 8 years

items: THE IDEA — BepiColombo is approaching the final stage of its journey to Mercury, the Solar System's innermost planet.
WHY NOW — A sequence of flybys and plasma-propulsion maneuvers has put the spacecraft on course for its decisive encounter later this year.
WHAT CHANGES — If it arrives at the right speed, Mercury's gravity will capture BepiColombo into orbit rather than letting it simply fly past.
THE CATCH — Reaching Mercury and slowing down takes more energy, or delta-v, than sending a spacecraft on a flyby to distant Pluto.
2018 — BepiColombo launches.
Since launch — The spacecraft uses plasma propulsion and flybys of Earth, Venus, and Mercury to reshape its trajectory.
Later this year — A final encounter is expected to place it into orbit around Mercury.

blocks.text: BepiColombo is a joint European Space Agency mission with contributions from Japan and the United States, costing nearly $2 billion.

Mercury is close to the Sun and moves quickly, so arriving there is not simply a matter of pointing a spacecraft inward. The mission must repeatedly adjust its velocity until the planet can capture it.
The payoff is close, but the physics has made the route unusually slow: reaching and orbiting Mercury demands more delta-v than a much farther Pluto flyby.

blocks.text: Competitive Pokémon is on phones, but top tournaments still require a Switch

Pokémon Champions works nearly the same across mobile and Switch, yet regional tournaments and above still exclude phone players. The stated reasons—visual quality and device complexity—do not fully explain the restriction.

blocks.caption: Champions downloads across platforms
blocks.text: 25 million

items: THE IDEA — You can build a tournament-ready team on mobile, with nearly the same battle experience as on Switch.
WHY NOW — From September 1, some local tournaments began allowing mobile, but regional events and the World Championships still require Switch hardware.
THE CATCH — Tournament officials cite Switch 2 graphics and the variety of mobile devices, even though streamed matches can use organizer-provided hardware.
WHAT CHANGES — Mobile players may qualify for the highest level of competition but still lack the device needed to compete there.

blocks.text: Pokémon Champions is built around accessibility, but its tournament rules stop short of that promise. Since battle calculations run on servers and team IDs can support streamed matches, the technical case for excluding mobile remains unclear. The result is a pathway where a player can start and progress on a phone, then face a Switch requirement at the biggest event.

Mobile is already used in high-level Pokémon Unite and Pokémon Go competition, even if those games have their own spectator and format limitations. With Switch 2 hardware becoming more expensive, keeping mobile out of elite VGC could exclude players who have the game—and the skill—but not the console.
Pokémon’s competitive scene is growing. Making the game accessible on phones is a strong start; letting that accessibility carry through to its biggest stages would make the rules match the message.

blocks.text: The Fairphone 6 Plus is an unusually ordinary Android phone—and that is its breakthrough.
Fairphone’s first proper US launch pairs familiar midrange performance with user-replaceable parts, long support and fewer compromises than earlier models.

items: THE IDEA — The 6 Plus feels much like a typical midrange Android phone, with clean software, competent cameras and a Snapdragon 7S Gen 4 chip.
WHY NOW — At $649, it is expensive for a midrange phone, but rising phone prices make its five-year warranty and up to six OS upgrades easier to justify.
WHAT CHANGES — Twelve parts, including the battery, screen, USB-C port and cameras, can be replaced by the owner. A new battery costs $39.99; a display costs $89.99.
THE CATCH — The phone has only IP55 protection, no wireless charging, modest speakers and merely adequate battery life, cameras and gaming performance.

blocks.text: The case for the 6 Plus is less about winning a specification contest than changing what ownership feels like. When the battery fades or a screen breaks, you can fix the phone yourself instead of treating it as disposable. Fairphone also adds swappable back panels and “Moments” focus modes, giving the device a little personality without loading it with gimmicks.
It is not the brightest, fastest or most water-resistant phone at this price. But it may be the first Fairphone that makes the responsible choice feel like a normal one.

blocks.text: The Fairphone 6 Plus is the midrange phone we desperately needed
Fairphone’s latest phone makes repairability feel less like a compromise: it offers familiar midrange performance, straightforward Android, and US availability.

items: THE IDEA — The 6 Plus is an ordinary-feeling Android phone with an unusual advantage: you can replace key parts yourself.
WHY NOW — Rising phone prices make its five-year warranty, up to six OS upgrades, and 12GB of RAM easier to justify.
WHAT CHANGES — Twelve user-replaceable parts include the battery, screen, USB-C port, and all three cameras. A battery costs $39.99 and a display costs $89.99.
THE CATCH — The IP55 rating, average battery life, speakers, display brightness, and camera system trail the best similarly priced phones.

blocks.text: The Fairphone 6 Plus is not the fastest or most polished phone at this price. Its case is that a phone can be merely good today and still make more sense years later, when a cheap battery or screen swap keeps it useful.
Repairability is finally part of the everyday phone experience, not a penalty for buying ethically.
For buyers who value longevity and easy repairs, the 6 Plus turns Fairphone’s ideals into a practical mainstream option—provided its compromises are acceptable.

blocks.text: Explore the globe in field recordings
Earth Garden turns Freesound’s environmental recordings into a quietly absorbing way to travel by ear.

blocks.caption: Earth Garden uses recordings from Freesound.
blocks.text: Around the world through environmental sound

items: THE IDEA — Spin a globe and listen to real environmental recordings from places including Atlantic islands, Tanzania and Manhattan.
WHY NOW — Earth Garden makes active listening feel effortless, whether you want to focus, work or wind down.
WHAT CHANGES — A reticle moves across the rotating globe and transitions between nearby sounds; optional ambient drones add a softer backdrop.
THE CATCH — Freesound’s library varies in quality and volume, with recordings concentrated in the US and Europe, especially the UK.

blocks.text: Earth Garden is essentially Radio Garden for the sounds around us: less about tuning into a station, more about noticing the texture of a place. I found the idea immediately appealing, particularly because the globe can rotate on its own while the audio changes beneath it.
A globe you can listen to, not just look at.

The uneven recordings are part of the trade-off. Some clips may be beautifully detailed, while others can be louder, rougher or simply more common in the catalogue. Still, the combination of geographic wandering and environmental audio makes Earth Garden an easy, soothing experiment in listening.
Try Earth Garden when you want a low-effort audio journey: let the globe turn, follow the changes in texture and treat the imperfections as part of the map.

blocks.text: Explore the globe in field recordings
Earth Garden turns Freesound’s environmental recordings into an interactive, audio-first trip around the planet.

blocks.caption: An interactive globe for environmental audio
blocks.text: Radio Garden, but for real-world sound

items: THE IDEA — Explore a rotating globe and hear field recordings from places including Atlantic islands, Tanzania and Manhattan.
WHY NOW — Earth Garden makes active listening feel geographic: move around the planet and the sound changes with the reticle.
WHAT CHANGES — The experience shifts between recordings as you browse, with optional generic ambient drones underneath.
THE CATCH — Freesound’s clips vary in quality and volume, and the collection is concentrated in the US and Europe, especially the UK.

blocks.text: Earth Garden is a simple but appealing twist on Radio Garden. Instead of tuning into live radio stations, you roam a globe of environmental audio: waves, crickets, rainfall and urban noise. Set it rotating automatically and the reticle moves into new recordings without requiring much effort from you.

The concept works because field recordings reward both background listening and close attention. The trade-off is the same openness that makes the project interesting: clips come from Freesound, so their polish and loudness are inconsistent. Still, it is a pleasing way to wander the world by ear.
A globe you explore one sound at a time.
